paragraphs: Most of the information a business keeps lives in tables, and SQL is the language you use to ask a table a question. You can ask which orders were the largest, which customers haven't bought anything yet, or how this month compares with last month. People who work with data in shops, schools and hospitals write queries like these every day, because the answers are already sitting in tables.

This course follows the records of one small shop. The first part teaches you to read a table properly: what a row stands for, how to pick the columns you want, keep only the rows that matter and put them in a sensible order. The second part boils many rows down to a count, a total or a group. The third joins tables together, and the fourth ranks and compares rows without throwing any away. The same few tables turn up in every lesson, so you soon know the data and can give your attention to the new idea.
Each lesson tells one idea as a short story. You work out what a query returns before you see the result.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what one row of a table stands for, and how a table tells its rows apart.
You'll be able to read a query and say exactly which rows and columns it returns.
You'll be able to summarise rows with counts, totals and averages, and say how missing values affect them.
You'll be able to follow a join between two tables and know which rows it keeps or drops.
You'll be able to rank rows, and work out running totals, without losing any rows.
prerequisites: You should be comfortable with everyday arithmetic and with reading rows and columns in a spreadsheet; no SQL is assumed.
